proof.text:
We must show that $\Delta_X \cup \bigcup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} R^n = \Delta_X \cup \bigcup_{n=1}^{|X|-1} R^n$, where the union on the right-hand side is understood to be empty when $|X| = 1$. Since the right-hand side is manifestly a subset of the left-hand side, it suffices to show that for every $(x, z) \in \bigcup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} R^n$, either $x = z$ or there exists an integer $m \in \{1, \dots, |X|-1\}$ such that $(x, z) \in R^m$.

    Let $(x, z) \in \bigcup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} R^n$ be given, and let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ be the least positive integer such that $(x, z) \in R^m$. If $x = z$, then $(x, z) \in \Delta_X$, and the claim holds. Suppose therefore that $x \neq z$. By the chain characterisation of $R^m$, there exists a sequence of elements $x = x_1, x_2, \dots, x_{m+1} = z$ in $X$ such that $(x_r, x_{r+1}) \in R$ for all $r \in \{1, \dots, m\}$.

    Suppose for contradiction that $m \ge |X|$. Then the sequence $x_1, \dots, x_{m+1}$ contains $m + 1 > |X|$ terms in $X$. By the pigeonhole principle, there exist indices $i, j \in \{1, \dots, m+1\}$ with $i < j$ such that $x_i = x_j$. Since $x_1 = x \neq z = x_{m+1}$, we cannot have both $i = 1$ and $j = m+1$. Consequently, omitting the intermediate terms $x_{i+1}, \dots, x_j$ yields a shorter chain
    \begin{align*}
        x = x_1, \dots, x_i, x_{j+1}, \dots, x_{m+1} = z
    \end{align*}
    of length $m^\prime = m - (j - i) \in \{1, \dots, m-1\}$ in which every consecutive pair belongs to $R$. Hence $(x, z) \in R^{m^\prime}$, contradicting the minimality of $m$. Therefore $m \le |X| - 1$, as desired.

proof.text:
First, we show that $\overset{\bm{x}}{\sim}$ is reflexive. For any $i \in \mathrm{domain}(\bm{x})$, we have $(i,i) \in \Delta_{\mathrm{domain}(\bm{x})}$, and since $\Delta_{\mathrm{domain}(\bm{x})} = \{(i,i) \mid i \in \mathrm{domain}(\bm{x})\}$ is a subset of the reflexive transitive closure, it follows that $i \overset{\bm{x}}{\sim} i$.

    Next, we show that $\overset{\bm{x}}{\sim}$ is symmetric. Suppose $i \overset{\bm{x}}{\sim} j$. Then, there exists a sequence of indices $i = i_1, i_2, \dots, i_n = j$ such that $i_k \overset{\bm{x}}{\leftrightsquigarrow} i_{k+1}$ for all $k < n$. Since $\overset{\bm{x}}{\leftrightsquigarrow}$ is symmetric, we have $i_{k+1} \overset{\bm{x}}{\leftrightsquigarrow} i_k$ for all $k < n$. Therefore, the sequence $j = i_n, i_{n-1}, \dots, i_1 = i$ shows that $j \overset{\bm{x}}{\sim} i$.

    Finally, we show that $\overset{\bm{x}}{\sim}$ is transitive. Suppose $i \overset{\bm{x}}{\sim} j$ and $j \overset{\bm{x}}{\sim} k$. Then, there exist sequences of indices $i = i_1, i_2, \dots, i_m = j$ and $j = j_1, j_2, \dots, j_p = k$ such that $i_r \overset{\bm{x}}{\leftrightsquigarrow} i_{r+1}$ for all $r < m$ and $j_l \overset{\bm{x}}{\leftrightsquigarrow} j_{l+1}$ for all $l < p$. Concatenating these sequences gives us a sequence of indices from $i$ to $k$, showing that $i \overset{\bm{x}}{\sim} k$.

proof.text:
By Proposition~\ref{prop:minimum-sorting-map-is-sorting-map}, $\varsigma_{\mathrm{min}}$ is a sorting map and its image lies in $\mathscr{S}(X,\preceq)$. We first note that the rule of Definition~\ref{defn:sorting-finite-sets} returns every sorted tuple unchanged, in the sense that if $\bm{z}\in\mathscr{S}(X,\preceq)$ and $\xi = \{(i_r,\bm{z}(r)) \mid r \in \mathrm{domain}(\bm{z})\}\in\mathscr{L}(X)$ with labels $i_1<\dots<i_{\ell(\bm{z})}$, then $\varsigma(\xi) = \bm{z}$. Indeed, suppose that the first $r-1$ steps have chosen the elements with labels $i_1,\dots,i_{r-1}$. Then $(i_r,\bm{z}(r))$ is minimal among the remaining elements, since $\bm{z}$ is sorted and so no later entry lies strictly below $\bm{z}(r)$, and it carries the smallest remaining label; it is therefore chosen at step $r$.

    Now let $\bm{x}\in\mathscr{T}(X)$ with $\ell(\bm{x})>0$, let $C_1,\dots,C_\kappa$ be the equivalence classes of $\overset{\bm{x}}{\sim}$ in order of first appearance, and let $\sigma$ be the bijection from the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:minimum-sorting-map-is-sorting-map}, so that $\bm{y} = \varsigma_{\mathrm{min}}(\bm{x}) = \bm{x}\circ\sigma$. Put $s_0 = 0$, $s_r = |C_1|+\dots+|C_r|$ and $B_r = \{s_{r-1}+1,\dots,s_r\}$. Then $\sigma(B_r) = C_r$, and the entries of $\bm{y}$ at the positions $B_r$ form the block $\varsigma(K_r)$.

    The comparability components of $\bm{y}$ are its blocks, in the same order. Comparability depends only on the entries, so $p \overset{\bm{y}}{\leftrightsquigarrow} q$ if and only if $\sigma(p) \overset{\bm{x}}{\leftrightsquigarrow} \sigma(q)$, and hence $p \overset{\bm{y}}{\sim} q$ if and only if $\sigma(p) \overset{\bm{x}}{\sim} \sigma(q)$. The equivalence classes of $\overset{\bm{y}}{\sim}$ are thus $\sigma^{-1}(C_r) = B_r$, and since $\min B_1 < \dots < \min B_\kappa$, the $r$-th comparability component of $\bm{y}$ is $\{(p,\bm{y}(p)) \mid p \in B_r\}$.

    This component lists the block $\varsigma(K_r)$ with increasing labels, and $\varsigma(K_r)$ is sorted by Definition~\ref{defn:sorting-finite-sets}, so by the observation above, sorting it returns $\varsigma(K_r)$. Hence
    \begin{align*}
        \varsigma_{\mathrm{min}}(\bm{y}) = \bigoplus_{r=1}^{\kappa}\varsigma(K_r) = \bm{y}.
    \end{align*}
    Together with $\varsigma_{\mathrm{min}}(\bm{e}) = \bm{e}$, this shows that $\varsigma_{\mathrm{min}}\circ\varsigma_{\mathrm{min}}=\varsigma_{\mathrm{min}}$.

We must show that $\varsigma : \mathscr{T}(X) \to \mathscr{S}(X,\preceq)$ is well-defined and satisfies the definition of a sorting map (Definition~\ref{defn:sorting-map}), namely that for every $\bm{x} \in \mathscr{T}(X)$, there exists a permutation $\pi \in \mathscr{P}_{\ell(\bm{x})}$ such that $\varsigma(\bm{x}) = \bm{x} \circ \pi \in \mathscr{S}(X,\preceq)$.

    First, by Lemma~\ref{lem:sorting-valid-first-choice-partition-covers}, the family $(\mathscr{U}_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is a pairwise disjoint cover of $\mathscr{T}(X)$. Consequently, every $\bm{x} \in \mathscr{T}(X)$ belongs to $\mathscr{U}_n$ for a unique index $n \in \mathbb{N}$, so the piecewise prescription for $\varsigma(\bm{x})$ is well-defined.

    Next, fix $\bm{x} \in \mathscr{T}(X)$ and let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ be the unique index such that $\bm{x} \in \mathscr{U}_n$. By definition of $\mathscr{U}_n$ and Definition~\ref{defn:sorting-valid-elements}, we have $\bm{x} \in \mathscr{U}_n \subseteq \mathscr{V}_{\pi_{(n)}}$, which implies that $\ell(\bm{x}) = \ell(\pi_{(n)})$ and $\bm{x} \circ \pi_{(n)} \in \mathscr{S}(X,\preceq)$. By Definition~\ref{defn:permutation-map}, it follows that
    \begin{align*}
        \varsigma(\bm{x}) = \varsigma_{\pi_{(n)}}(\bm{x}) = \bm{x}[\pi_{(n)}] = \bm{x} \circ \pi_{(n)} \in \mathscr{S}(X,\preceq),
    \end{align*}
    with $\pi_{(n)} \in \mathscr{P}_{\ell(\bm{x})}$. Therefore, $\varsigma$ is a sorting map, as desired.

environments.statement: Note that the measurability results below require only that the order relation belong to the Borel $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal{B}(X\times X)$ of the product topology, and therefore require neither completeness nor separability of $X$. Separability becomes important when measurable maps into $X\times X$ are constructed componentwise from maps into each coordinate. For instance, if $\xi$ and $\eta$ are $X$-valued random elements on a measurable space $(\Omega, \mathcal{F})$, then the paired map $\omega \mapsto (\xi(\omega), \eta(\omega))$ is $(\mathcal{F}, \mathcal{B}(X)\otimes\mathcal{B}(X))$-measurable; consequently, the comparison set $\{\omega \in \Omega \mid \xi(\omega) \preceq \eta(\omega)\}$ is guaranteed to be an event in $\mathcal{F}$ whenever $\mathcal{B}(X\times X)=\mathcal{B}(X)\otimes\mathcal{B}(X)$, which holds when $X$ is separable, whereas without separability even the diagonal $\Delta_X$ may fail to lie in $\mathcal{B}(X)\otimes\mathcal{B}(X)$.

proof.text:
We must show that the composite mapping $\mathscr{Q}_{\mathrm{state}}:\mathscr{T}(O)\to[0,\infty)$ is Borel measurable. First, note that the separation map $\bm{m} \mapsto (\bm{b}, \bm{s})$ is continuous by Proposition~\ref{prop:separation-continuous}, and the coordinate projections $(\bm{b}, \bm{s}) \mapsto ((\bm{p}^{\bm{b}}, \bm{q}^{\bm{b}}), (\bm{p}^{\bm{s}}, \bm{q}^{\bm{s}}))$ are continuous by Proposition~\ref{prop:tuple-projection-continuous}, so their composition is Borel measurable.

    Second, on the zero-length layer $\{\bm{e}\} \times \{\bm{e}\}$, each sorted-pair map $(\bm{p}, \bm{q}) \mapsto (\bm{p}[\pi^\preceq(\bm{p})], \bm{q}[\pi^\preceq(\bm{p})])$ is constant at $(\bm{e}, \bm{e})$ and hence Borel measurable. On each positive-length matching layer $\mathbb{R}^n \times [0,\infty)^n$ with $n \in \mathbb{N}$, Proposition~\ref{prop:minimal-sorting-measurable} establishes that $\bm{p} \mapsto \pi^\preceq(\bm{p})$ is Borel measurable, and Proposition~\ref{prop:permuting-continuous} establishes that the permutation map $(\bm{x}, \pi) \mapsto \bm{x}[\pi]$ is continuous. Because the fixed-length layers of $\mathscr{T}(\mathbb{R})$ and $\mathscr{T}([0,\infty))$ are clopen by the \hyperref[thm:the-standard-machinery]{standard machinery} (Theorem~\ref{thm:the-standard-machinery}), the matching-length product layers form a countable Borel partition of the matching-length domain, and Theorem~\ref{thm:measurable-partition} pastes the layerwise maps into Borel measurable maps $\bm{m} \mapsto (\widehat{\bm{p}}^{\bm{b}}, \widehat{\bm{q}}^{\bm{b}})$ and $\bm{m} \mapsto (\widehat{\bm{p}}^{\bm{s}}, \widehat{\bm{q}}^{\bm{s}})$.

    Third, by Lemma~\ref{lem:cumulative-summation-continuous}, the cumulative summation map $\bm{\Sigma} : \mathscr{T}([0,\infty)) \to \mathscr{T}([0,\infty))$ is continuous. Since the sorted price tuples $\widehat{\bm{p}}^{\bm{s}}$ and $\widehat{\bm{p}}^{\bm{b}}$ belong to $\mathscr{S}(\mathbb{R}, \leq)$ and $\mathscr{S}(\mathbb{R}, \geq)$, the cumulative quantities $\widehat{\bm{Q}}^{\bm{s}}$ and $\widehat{\bm{Q}}^{\bm{b}}$ are non-decreasing, and reindexing together with $\bm{\Sigma}$ preserves tuple lengths, the image of the map
    \begin{align*}
        \bm{m} \mapsto \Bigl(\bigl(\widehat{\bm{Q}}^{\bm{s}}(\bm{m}), \widehat{\bm{p}}^{\bm{s}}(\bm{m})\bigr), \bigl(\widehat{\bm{Q}}^{\bm{b}}(\bm{m}), \widehat{\bm{p}}^{\bm{b}}(\bm{m})\bigr)\Bigr)
    \end{align*}
    lies in $\mathfrak{C}(\leq) \times \mathfrak{C}(\geq)$. By the product identity for Borel $\sigma$-algebras on separable metric spaces noted in Subsection~\ref{subsec:step-3-sorting}, componentwise measurability implies that this map is Borel measurable into $\mathfrak{C}(\leq) \times \mathfrak{C}(\geq)$. Composing it with the Borel measurable functional $\mathscr{Q}$ of Theorem~\ref{thm:equilibrium-quantity-measurable} proves that $\mathscr{Q}_{\mathrm{state}}$ is Borel measurable, as desired.

    &\bm{s} &= \bm{\Pi}_{\mathrm{sell}}\bm{m},\\
    \bm{p}^{\bm{b}} &= \bm{P}_1\bm{b},
    &\bm{q}^{\bm{b}} &= \bm{P}_2\bm{b},\\
    \bm{p}^{\bm{s}} &= \bm{P}_1\bm{s},
    &\bm{q}^{\bm{s}} &= \bm{P}_2\bm{s},
\end{align*}
and define the sorted pairs by
\begin{align*}
    (\widehat{\bm{p}}^{\bm{b}},\widehat{\bm{q}}^{\bm{b}})
    &=\bigl(\bm{p}^{\bm{b}}[\pi^\geq(\bm{p}^{\bm{b}})],
    \bm{q}^{\bm{b}}[\pi^\geq(\bm{p}^{\bm{b}})]\bigr),\\
    (\widehat{\bm{p}}^{\bm{s}},\widehat{\bm{q}}^{\bm{s}})
    &=\bigl(\bm{p}^{\bm{s}}[\pi^\leq(\bm{p}^{\bm{s}})],
    \bm{q}^{\bm{s}}[\pi^\leq(\bm{p}^{\bm{s}})]\bigr),
\end{align*}
where $\pi^\preceq(\bm{e})$ is the unique empty permutation. Let
\begin{align*}
    \widehat{\bm{Q}}^{\bm{b}}=\bm{\Sigma}(\widehat{\bm{q}}^{\bm{b}}),
    \qquad
    \widehat{\bm{Q}}^{\bm{s}}=\bm{\Sigma}(\widehat{\bm{q}}^{\bm{s}}),
\end{align*}
and define
\begin{align*}
    \mathscr{Q}_{\mathrm{state}}(\bm{m})
    =\mathscr{Q}\bigl((\widehat{\bm{Q}}^{\bm{s}},\widehat{\bm{p}}^{\bm{s}}),
    (\widehat{\bm{Q}}^{\bm{b}},\widehat{\bm{p}}^{\bm{b}})\bigr).
\end{align*}
Then $\mathscr{Q}_{\mathrm{state}}:\mathscr{T}(O)\to[0,\infty)$ is Borel measurable.

proof.text:
We must show that for every $\bm{m} \in \mathscr{T}(O)$ and every permutation $\rho \in \mathscr{P}_{\ell(\bm{m})}$, it holds that $\mathscr{Q}_{\mathrm{state}}(\bm{m}\circ\rho)=\mathscr{Q}_{\mathrm{state}}(\bm{m})$ and $\mathscr{P}_{\mathrm{state}}(\bm{m}\circ\rho)=\mathscr{P}_{\mathrm{state}}(\bm{m})$. For each $p\in\mathbb{R}$, let $S_{\bm{m}}(p)$ denote the total quantity of the sell orders in $\bm{m}$ with price at most $p$, and let $D_{\bm{m}}(p)$ denote the total quantity of the buy orders in $\bm{m}$ with price at least $p$. Since both quantities are finite sums over the entries of $\bm{m}$, reindexing by the bijection $\rho$ leaves them unchanged, so that $S_{\bm{m}\circ\rho}(p)=S_{\bm{m}}(p)$ and $D_{\bm{m}\circ\rho}(p)=D_{\bm{m}}(p)$ for all $p \in \mathbb{R}$. Applying Proposition~\ref{prop:executable-volume-uniform-price} to the sorted pairs of Corollary~\ref{cor:state-compatible-volume-measurable} yields
    \begin{align*}
        \mathscr{Q}_{\mathrm{state}}(\bm{m}\circ\rho)
        = \max_{p\in\mathbb{R}}\min\bigl(S_{\bm{m}\circ\rho}(p),D_{\bm{m}\circ\rho}(p)\bigr)
        = \max_{p\in\mathbb{R}}\min\bigl(S_{\bm{m}}(p),D_{\bm{m}}(p)\bigr)
        = \mathscr{Q}_{\mathrm{state}}(\bm{m}),
    \end{align*}
    which proves the first identity.

    To prove the second identity, let $Q=\mathscr{Q}_{\mathrm{state}}(\bm{m})=\mathscr{Q}_{\mathrm{state}}(\bm{m}\circ\rho)$. If $Q=0$, then $\mathscr{P}_{\mathrm{state}}(\bm{m}\circ\rho) = 0 = \mathscr{P}_{\mathrm{state}}(\bm{m})$ by definition. Assume therefore that $Q>0$, and write $\iota=\iota^{\bm{s}}(\bm{m})$. Every sell order with a price strictly below $\widehat{\bm{p}}^{\bm{s}}(\iota)$ precedes position $\iota$ in the sorted sell tuple, so for any $p<\widehat{\bm{p}}^{\bm{s}}(\iota)$, the cumulative sell quantity $S_{\bm{m}}(p)$ is at most the cumulative sell quantity strictly before position $\iota$, which is strictly less than $Q$ by the minimality of $\iota$. Conversely, at $p = \widehat{\bm{p}}^{\bm{s}}(\iota)$, we have $S_{\bm{m}}(\widehat{\bm{p}}^{\bm{s}}(\iota))\geq\widehat{\bm{Q}}^{\bm{s}}(\iota)\geq Q$. Consequently,
    \begin{align*}
        \widehat{\bm{p}}^{\bm{s}}(\iota^{\bm{s}}(\bm{m}))=\min\{p\in\mathbb{R}\mid S_{\bm{m}}(p)\geq Q\},
        \qquad
        \widehat{\bm{p}}^{\bm{b}}(\iota^{\bm{b}}(\bm{m}))=\max\{p\in\mathbb{R}\mid D_{\bm{m}}(p)\geq Q\},
    \end{align*}
    where the second characterisation follows by a symmetric argument on the buy side. Because the right-hand sides depend on $\bm{m}$ solely through $S_{\bm{m}}$, $D_{\bm{m}}$, and $Q$, each of which is invariant under $\rho$, their arithmetic mean $\mathscr{P}_{\mathrm{state}}(\bm{m})$ satisfies $\mathscr{P}_{\mathrm{state}}(\bm{m}\circ\rho)=\mathscr{P}_{\mathrm{state}}(\bm{m})$, as desired.

proof.text:
We must show that for every $\bm{x} \in \mathscr{T}(X)$, every $\bm{x}^\prime \in \bm{x}^\pi$, and every Borel set $B \in \mathcal{B}(X)$, it holds that $\mathfrak{m}(\bm{x}^\prime)(B) = \mathfrak{m}(\bm{x})(B)$. If $\bm{x} = \bm{e}$, then $\bm{x}^\pi = \{\bm{e}\}$ and the identity is immediate. Suppose therefore that $\ell(\bm{x}) > 0$. By Definition~\ref{defn:permutative-equality}, any $\bm{x}^\prime \in \bm{x}^\pi$ satisfies $\ell(\bm{x}^\prime) = \ell(\bm{x})$ and $\bm{x}^\prime = \bm{x} \circ \sigma$ for some permutation $\sigma \in \mathscr{P}_{\ell(\bm{x})}$.         = \sum_{j \in \mathrm{domain}(\bm{x})} \delta_{\bm{x}(j)}(B)
        = \mathfrak{m}(\bm{x})(B),

    which proves that $\mathfrak{m}(\bm{x}^\prime) = \mathfrak{m}(\bm{x})$, as desired.

proof.text:
We must show first that for all $(q_f,p_f),(q_g,p_g)\in\mathcal{A}$ and all $\alpha,\beta\geq0$, the linear combination $\alpha(q_f,p_f)+\beta(q_g,p_g)$ belongs to $\mathcal{A}$, and second that for every $(q,p)\in\mathcal{A}$, the formula \eqref{eq:graph-wise-decoder} defines a unique element $D(q,p)\in\mathpzc{P}$ on $\mathrm{image}(q)$.

    Let $(q_f,p_f),(q_g,p_g)\in\mathcal{A}$ and $\alpha,\beta\geq0$ be given, and set
    \begin{align*}
        q=\alpha q_f+\beta q_g,
        \qquad
        p=\alpha p_f+\beta p_g.
    \end{align*}
    Then $q$ is continuous and increasing with $q(0)=0$, the functions $q$ and $p$ are affine on the cells of a common finite partition of $[-1,1]$, and $p$ is increasing. Right-continuity on $[-1,1)$ is preserved under non-negative linear combinations. Moreover, the terminal plateau of $q$ begins at the latest terminal-plateau start among the components with a strictly positive coefficient. At that point, components with an earlier start are already constant and the remaining components satisfy their left-limit condition, so $p$ satisfies condition~(4) of Definition~\ref{defn:graph-tracing-pairs} as well. To verify condition~(3), suppose that $u,v\in[-1,1]$ satisfy $u<v$ and $q(u)=q(v)$. Then
    \begin{align*}
        0
        =q(v)-q(u)
        =\alpha\bigl(q_f(v)-q_f(u)\bigr)
        +\beta\bigl(q_g(v)-q_g(u)\bigr).
    \end{align*}
    As in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:linear-parametrisation-convex}, every component with a strictly positive coefficient is constant on $[u,v]$, and hence $p(u)=p(v)$. Consequently, $(q,p)\in\mathcal{A}$, which proves that $\mathcal{A}$ is a convex cone.

    For the second claim, let $(q,p)\in\mathcal{A}$ be given. Because $p$ takes the same value at every pair $u,v\in[-1,1]$ satisfying $q(u)=q(v)$, the rule \eqref{eq:graph-wise-decoder} is well-defined on $\mathrm{image}(q)$. Since $q$ and $p$ are increasing, the decoded function $D(q,p)$ is increasing. Furthermore, $D(q,p)$ is affine on the image of every cell on which $q$ is not constant, so it is piecewise affine, and it is simple whenever $p$ is simple. It inherits the one-sided continuity convention chosen at the start of this section from condition~(4) on $p$, and its graph is exactly $\mathrm{image}(u\mapsto(q(u),p(u)))$, which establishes uniqueness, as desired.

We establish the bound by rescaling an arbitrary feasible element of $\mathcal{A}_{\alpha\mathcal{G}}(\alpha q_{\mathrm{start}}, \alpha q_{\mathrm{stop}}; \widehat{\bm{P}}_d)$ and exploiting the monotonicity of $\widehat{P}_{d,h}$. By construction, $\Delta\widetilde{q}_h \in \mathcal{R}$ and the cumulative sums satisfy $\widetilde{q}_h = q_{\mathrm{start}} + \sum_{r=1}^h \Delta\widetilde{q}_r = \alpha^{-1}q_h \in \mathcal{G}$ for all $h$, with $\widetilde{q}_{24} = q_{\mathrm{stop}}$. Thus $\Delta\widetilde{\bm{q}} \in \mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{G}}(q_{\mathrm{start}}, q_{\mathrm{stop}}; \widehat{\bm{P}}_d)$.

Next, fix $h \in \{1,\dots,24\}$. Since $\alpha > 1$ and $\widehat{P}_{d,h}$ is non-decreasing, if $\tau(\Delta q_h) \geq 0$, then $0 \leq \tau(\Delta\widetilde{q}_h) \leq \tau(\Delta q_h)$ implies $\widehat{P}_{d,h}(\tau(\Delta\widetilde{q}_h)) \leq \widehat{P}_{d,h}(\tau(\Delta q_h))$; multiplying by the non-positive quantity $-\tau(\Delta q_h) = -\alpha\tau(\Delta\widetilde{q}_h)$ reverses the inequality. \begin{align*}

We verify the Borel measurability of each constituent map in Definition~\ref{defn:depth-restricted-step}. First, the composite action application map $(\bm{m},\bm{c})\mapsto\bm{m}\lhd\bm{c}$ is continuous and hence Borel measurable by Theorem~\ref{thm:composite-application-continuous}. Second, the price--time priority relation $\preceq$ of \eqref{eq:price-time-priority} has a Borel-measurable graph in $O\times O$ because it is defined by Boolean combinations of coordinate equalities and strict inequalities, so the minimum sorting map $\varsigma:\mathscr{T}(O)\to\mathscr{S}(O,\preceq)$ is Borel measurable by Theorem~\ref{thm:minimal-sorting-measurable}. Composing these two maps shows that $(\bm{m},\bm{c})\mapsto\widetilde{\bm{m}}=\varsigma(\bm{m}\lhd\bm{c})$ is jointly Borel measurable.

    Third, on $\mathscr{S}(O,\preceq)$, the side separation operators $\bm{\Pi}_{\mathrm{buy}}$ and $\bm{\Pi}_{\mathrm{sell}}$ are continuous by Proposition~\ref{prop:separation-continuous}. For each side $\kappa\in\{\mathrm{buy},\mathrm{sell}\}$, restricting a tuple $\bm{x}\in\mathscr{S}(U,\preceq^\kappa)$ to the first $100$ indices via $\bm{x}\mapsto\bm{x}[\{1,\dots,100\}]$ and extracting its latent tail via $\bm{x}\mapsto\bm{x}[\operatorname{domain}(\bm{x})\setminus\{1,\dots,100\}]$ are continuous on each fixed-length layer $U^n$ and hence Borel measurable by the standard machinery (Theorem~\ref{thm:the-standard-machinery}), Corollary~\ref{cor:filter}, and Proposition~\ref{prop:characteristic-functions-tuple}.     Finally, the clearing operator $\mathsf{C}:\mathscr{S}(O,\preceq)\to\mathscr{S}(O,\preceq)$ is Borel measurable by Theorem~\ref{thm:clearing-measurable}. Conversely, if $\sum_{i\in\mathcal{R}} x_{i,j}+\sum_{u\in\mathcal{A}} y_{u,j}\le 1$, then at most one variable among $\{x_{i,j}\}_{i\in\mathcal{R}}\cup\{y_{u,j}\}_{u\in\mathcal{A}}$ equals $1$; setting $\beta_j = \sum_{i\in\mathcal{R}} x_{i,j}\in\{0,1\}$ satisfies both channel inequalities.

    Second, consider any feasible solution $(x,y,\beta,z)$ of the global problem~\eqref{eq:intraday-global-matching-objective}. By the block-link constraints $x_{i,j}\le z_{I_k,J_l}$ and $y_{u,j}\le z_{I_k,J_l}$, nonzero assignments can occur only within block pairs $(I_k,J_l)$ for which $z_{I_k,J_l}=1$ and $\lvert\sigma_k-\tilde{\sigma}_l\rvert\le\delta_t$. Because the blocks $(I_k)_{k=1}^N$ partition $\{1,\dots,n\}$ and $(J_l)_{l=1}^M$ partition $\{1,\dots,m\}$, the capacity constraints $\sum_{j=1}^m x_{i,j}\tilde{q}_j\le\Delta q_i$ and the assignment constraints decouple across distinct linked pairs $(I_k,J_l)$. Maximising over $(x,y,\beta)$ for a fixed feasible link matrix $z$ therefore yields the objective value $\sum_{(k,l):z_{I_k,J_l}=1}\mathsf{Match}_{I_k,J_l}$; a link with $\mathsf{Match}_{I_k,J_l}=0$ contributes nothing and may be reset to $z_{I_k,J_l}=0$ without violating any constraint, so we may assume that every selected link carries a strictly positive assignment. Finally, the degree constraints $\sum_{k=1}^N z_{I_k,J_l}\le 1$ and $\sum_{l=1}^M z_{I_k,J_l}\le 1$ together with the non-crossing constraint $z_{I_k,J_l}+z_{I_{k'},J_{l'}}\le 1$ ($k<k'$, $l>l'$) characterise precisely the set of strictly increasing sequences of block pairs $1\le k_1<\cdots<k_r\le N$ and $1\le l_1<\cdots<l_r\le M$. By standard dynamic-programming induction on $(k,l)$, the maximum of $\sum_{s=1}^r \mathsf{Match}_{I_{k_s},J_{l_s}}$ over all such strictly increasing pair sequences on $\{1,\dots,k\}\times\{1,\dots,l\}$ satisfies the recursion~\eqref{eq:intraday-outer-dp-main}, and hence $V_{N,M}$ equals the global maximum of~\eqref{eq:intraday-global-matching-objective}.

proof.text:
We must show that the minimisers in~\eqref{eq:quantity-pava} and~\eqref{eq:price-pava} exist and are unique, that they leave any representative $z=(a,c)=\mathsf{A}(F)$ of a non-decreasing pair $F=(\psi,\phi)$ with $\phi([-1,1])\subseteq[\underline{p},\overline{p}]$ invariant, and that $\bm{p}(\widetilde{z})$ is non-expansive with respect to the weighted Euclidean norm on $\mathbb{R}^{1000}$.

First, define the monotony cone $C_q=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{1001}\mid x_{-m}\leq\cdots\leq x_m\}$ and the bounded monotony set $C_p=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^{1000}\mid \underline{p}\leq y_{-m+1}\leq\cdots\leq y_m\leq\overline{p}\}$. Both sets are non-empty, closed, and convex in their respective Euclidean spaces. Because the weights $w_j$ in~\eqref{eq:quantity-pava} are strictly positive, the quadratic forms $\sum_{j=-m}^{m}w_j(x_j-\widetilde{a}_j)^2$ and $\sum_{j=-m+1}^{m}(y_j-\widetilde{c}_j)^2$ are squared norms induced by weighted Euclidean inner products. By the Hilbert projection theorem on finite-dimensional spaces, the metric projections $\bm{q}(\widetilde{z})$ onto $C_q$ and $\bm{p}(\widetilde{z})$ onto $C_p$ exist and are unique.

Second, let $z=(a,c)=\mathsf{A}(F)$ be the numerical representative of a non-decreasing function pair $F=(\psi,\phi)$ with $\phi([-1,1])\subseteq[\underline{p},\overline{p}]$. Because $\psi$ and $\phi$ are non-decreasing, the node values satisfy $a_{-m}\leq\cdots\leq a_m$ and the cell averages satisfy $\underline{p}\leq c_{-m+1}\leq\cdots\leq c_m\leq\overline{p}$. Hence $a\in C_q$ and $c\in C_p$, so the metric projections onto $C_q$ and $C_p$ leave $a$ and $c$ unchanged.

Finally, because metric projection onto the closed convex set $C_p$ in $\mathbb{R}^{1000}$ equipped with the standard Euclidean norm (and hence under positive rescaling by $h>0$) is $1$-Lipschitz and fixes $c\in C_p$, it holds that
\begin{align*}
\sum_{j=-m+1}^{m}h\,\bigl((\bm{p}(\widetilde{z}))_j-c_j\bigr)^2
= h\,\bigl\lVert\bm{p}(\widetilde{z})-\bm{p}(z)\bigr\rVert_2^2
\leq h\,\lVert\widetilde{c}-c\rVert_2^2
= \sum_{j=-m+1}^{m}h\,\bigl(\widetilde{c}_j-c_j\bigr)^2,
\end{align*}
as desired.

environments.title: Existence, Uniqueness, and Non-Expansiveness of Coordinate Isotonic Decoding

proof.text:
We must show that the integral $\int_{-1}^{1}\bigl(\phi_a(u)\phi_{a'}(u)+\pi_c(u)\pi_{c'}(u)\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}u$ coincides with the sum in~\eqref{eq:numerical-inner-product}.

Fix a cell $K_j=[u_{j-1},u_j]$ of width $h=u_j-u_{j-1}$. Using the local coordinate $s=(u-u_{j-1})/h\in[0,1]$, the linear interpolants on $K_j$ take the form $\phi_a(u)=(1-s)a_{j-1}+sa_j$ and $\phi_{a'}(u)=(1-s)a'_{j-1}+sa'_j$. Changing variables to $s$ with $\mathrm{d}u=h\,\mathrm{d}s$ and using the elementary integrals $\int_0^1(1-s)^2\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_0^1 s^2\,\mathrm{d}s=1/3$ and $\int_0^1 s(1-s)\,\mathrm{d}s=1/6$, we obtain
\begin{align*}
\int_{K_j}\phi_a(u)\phi_{a'}(u)\,\mathrm{d}u
&= h\int_0^1\bigl((1-s)a_{j-1}+sa_j\bigr)\bigl((1-s)a'_{j-1}+sa'_j\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}s\\
&= \frac{h}{6}\bigl(2a_{j-1}a'_{j-1}+a_{j-1}a'_j+a_ja'_{j-1}+2a_ja'_j\bigr).
\end{align*}
Similarly, because $\pi_c$ and $\pi_{c'}$ are constant and equal to $c_j$ and $c'_j$ on the interior of $K_j$, their product integrates to $\int_{K_j}\pi_c(u)\pi_{c'}(u)\,\mathrm{d}u=h\,c_jc'_j$. Summing both cell integrals over $j\in\{-m+1,\ldots,m\}$ yields~\eqref{eq:numerical-inner-product}, as desired.

We establish properties (i), (ii), and (iii) in turn.

    For (i), associativity and commutativity descend from componentwise addition on $X\times X$, and $[(x,y)]+[(e,e)]=[(x,y)]$. If $(x,y)\sim(x^\prime,y^\prime)$, then commutativity gives $y+x^\prime=y^\prime+x$, so $(y,x)\sim(y^\prime,x^\prime)$, and the class $[(y,x)]$ does not depend on the representative of $[(x,y)]$. Moreover, $[(x,y)]+[(y,x)]=[(x+y,y+x)]=[(e,e)]$, since $(x+y)+e=e+(y+x)$ by the identity law and commutativity.

    For (ii), $\iota(x+x^\prime)=[(x+x^\prime,e+e)]=\iota(x)+\iota(x^\prime)$, and $\iota(e)=[(e,e)]$ is the identity element of $G(X)$. If $\iota(x)=\iota(x^\prime)$, then $(x,e)\sim(x^\prime,e)$, that is, $x+e=x^\prime+e$, and hence $x=x^\prime$. Finally, by (i), $\iota(x)-\iota(y)=[(x,e)]+[(e,y)]=[(x,y)]$.

    For (iii), if $(x,y)\sim(x^\prime,y^\prime)$, then $\psi(x)+\psi(y^\prime)=\psi(x^\prime)+\psi(y)$, so $\psi(x)-\psi(y)=\psi(x^\prime)-\psi(y^\prime)$, and $\bar{\psi}$ is well-defined. It is additive because $\psi$ is additive, $\bar{\psi}([(e,e)])=\psi(e)-\psi(e)=0$, and $\bar{\psi}(\iota(x))=\psi(x)-\psi(e)=\psi(x)$. If $\chi:G(X)\to H$ is any monoid homomorphism with $\chi\circ\iota=\psi$, then $\chi$ preserves inverses, and (ii) gives $\chi([(x,y)])=\chi(\iota(x))-\chi(\iota(y))=\psi(x)-\psi(y)$, so $\chi=\bar{\psi}$, as desired.

Definition~\ref{defn:completed-kernel-space} and Corollary~\ref{cor:grothendieck-vectorization-inner-product-space} use metric completion to add limits of Cauchy sequences; this is distinct from group completion. proof.text:
We must show that the maximum map defines a pseudometric (and a metric when each $d_i$ is a metric) that induces the product topology and inherits separability and completeness from the factors. The maximum vanishes on the diagonal and is symmetric because every $d_i$ is, and the triangle inequality holds in each coordinate and therefore for the maximum; if every $d_i$ is a metric, vanishing of the maximum implies equality in every coordinate. Next, the ball of radius $\varepsilon$ around $\bm{x}$ is $\prod_{i=1}^n B^{d_i}_\varepsilon(\bm{x}(i))$, which is open in the product topology. Conversely, if $\bm{x}\in\prod_{i=1}^n O_i$ with each $O_i$ open in $X_i$, choose $\varepsilon_i>0$ with $B^{d_i}_{\varepsilon_i}(\bm{x}(i))\subseteq O_i$; the ball of radius $\min_i\varepsilon_i$ around $\bm{x}$ then lies in $\prod_{i=1}^n O_i$. By the centred-ball characterisation following Proposition~\ref{prop:topology-extended-pseudometric}, the two topologies coincide.

    Finally, if $D_i\subseteq X_i$ is countable and dense for each $i$, then $\prod_{i=1}^n D_i$ is countable and dense, since for $\bm{x}$ and $\varepsilon>0$ we may choose $y_i\in D_i$ with $d_i(\bm{x}(i),y_i)<\varepsilon$ for every $i$. If $(\bm{x}_m)_{m\in\mathbb{N}}$ is Cauchy, then so is each coordinate sequence. If every factor is complete, their limits $x_i\in X_i$ form $\bm{x}=(x_1,\dots,x_n)$, and $\bm{x}_m\to\bm{x}$ in every coordinate and hence in the maximum metric, as desired.

proof.text:
We must show that $d_\infty$ is a metric on $C([a,b];X)$ and that $(C([a,b];X),d_\infty)$ inherits completeness and separability from $(X,d)$. The metric axioms pass from $d$ to $d_\infty$ pointwise in $t$. For the triangle inequality, let $f,g,h\in C([a,b];X)$; then
    \begin{align*}
        d(f(t),h(t))\leq d(f(t),g(t))+d(g(t),h(t))\leq d_\infty(f,g)+d_\infty(g,h)
    \end{align*}
    for every $t\in[a,b]$, and taking the supremum over $t$ gives $d_\infty(f,h)\leq d_\infty(f,g)+d_\infty(g,h)$.

    Suppose that $(X,d)$ is complete, and let $(f_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be Cauchy under $d_\infty$. For each $t\in[a,b]$, the sequence $(f_n(t))_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ is Cauchy in $X$ and hence converges to some $f(t)\in X$. Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose $N\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $d_\infty(f_m,f_n)<\varepsilon$ for all $m,n\geq N$; letting $m\to\infty$ gives $d(f_n(t),f(t))\leq\varepsilon$ for all $n\geq N$ and $t\in[a,b]$. Fix $n\geq N$ and $t_0\in[a,b]$, and choose $\delta>0$ such that $d(f_n(t),f_n(t_0))<\varepsilon$ whenever $|t-t_0|<\delta$. For such $t$, the triangle inequality gives $d(f(t),f(t_0))<3\varepsilon$. Hence $f$ is continuous and $d_\infty(f_n,f)\leq\varepsilon$ for all $n\geq N$, so $(C([a,b];X),d_\infty)$ is complete.

    Suppose that $(X,d)$ is separable, and let $D\subseteq X$ be countable and dense. For points $a=s_0<s_1<\dots<s_m=b$ with $s_1,\dots,s_{m-1}\in\mathbb{Q}$, centres $y_1,\dots,y_m\in D$, and a rational radius $q>0$, consider the set of all $g\in C([a,b];X)$ with $g([s_{k-1},s_k])\subseteq B_q(y_k)$ for $k=1,\dots,m$. There are countably many such sets, and we choose one element from each non-empty one. Let $f\in C([a,b];X)$ and $\varepsilon>0$. Since $[a,b]$ is compact, $f$ is uniformly continuous, so we may choose the points $s_k$ such that $d(f(s),f(t))<\varepsilon$ whenever $s,t\in[s_{k-1},s_k]$. Choose $y_k\in D$ with $d(f(s_k),y_k)<\varepsilon$ and a rational $q\in(2\varepsilon,3\varepsilon)$. Then $f$ lies in the corresponding set, so the element $g$ chosen from it satisfies $d(f(t),g(t))\leq d(f(t),y_k)+d(y_k,g(t))<5\varepsilon$ for $t\in[s_{k-1},s_k]$. Hence $d_\infty(f,g)\leq5\varepsilon$, and the chosen elements form a countable dense subset.

proof.text: We must show that $\Gamma(f)$ is compact, closed, and bounded in $([a,b]\times X,\rho)$. Define $\Phi:[a,b] \to [a,b] \times X$ by $\Phi(t) = (t,f(t))$. Continuity of $f$ implies that $\Phi$ is continuous under $\rho$. The interval $[a,b]$ is compact, so its continuous image $\Phi([a,b]) = \Gamma(f)$ is compact. Every metric space in the sense of Remark~\ref{rem:extended-metric-convention} is Hausdorff, so the compact set $\Gamma(f)$ is closed. On that component, $\rho$ is an ordinary metric, so compactness implies that $\Gamma(f)$ is bounded, as desired.

environments.optionalTitle: Regular paths are bounded and Borel

proof.text:
We first show boundedness. Fix $x_0\in X$ and suppose, for contradiction, that $d(x_0,f(t_k))\to\infty$ along a sequence $(t_k)_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\subseteq[a,b]$. Since $[a,b]$ is compact, we may pass to a monotone subsequence converging to some $t\in[a,b]$, and since $f(t)$ is a single point, we may further assume that the subsequence is strictly monotone. If it is increasing, the left limit $f(t-)$ exists, and if it is decreasing, the right limit $f(t+)$ exists: a c\`adl\`ag function has left limits and is right-continuous, a c\`agl\`ad function has right limits and is left-continuous, and a continuous function has both one-sided limits. In either case $d(x_0,f(t_k))$ converges to the finite number $d(x_0,f(t\mp))$, a contradiction.

    We now show Borel measurability. Let $f\in D^+([a,b];X)$. For $m\in\mathbb{N}$ put $t_j=a+j(b-a)/m$ for $j\in\{0,\dots,m\}$, and define $f_m(t)=f(t_j)$ for $t\in[t_{j-1},t_j)$ with $j\in\{1,\dots,m\}$, together with $f_m(b)=f(b)$. Each $f_m$ takes finitely many values, each on a Borel subset of $[a,b]$, and is therefore Borel measurable. For $t\in[a,b)$ the node $t_j$ chosen at stage $m$ satisfies $t<t_j\leq t+(b-a)/m$, so $t_j\downarrow t$ and right-continuity gives $f_m(t)\to f(t)$; at $t=b$ the sequence is constant. A pointwise limit of Borel measurable maps into a metric space is Borel measurable, since for an open set $U\subseteq X$ and $U_k=\{x\in X\mid d(x,X\setminus U)>1/k\}$ one has $\{t\mid f(t)\in U\}=\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\bigcup_{N\in\mathbb{N}}\bigcap_{m\geq N}\{t\mid f_m(t)\in U_k\}$. Hence $f$ is Borel measurable. For $f\in D^-([a,b];X)$ the same argument applies with the cells $(t_{j-1},t_j]$, the values $f_m(t)=f(t_{j-1})$, $f_m(a)=f(a)$, and left-continuity, and a continuous $f$ is Borel measurable as a continuous map.

proof.text:
We prove the three claims in order. For (i), since $[0]\in\mathcal{C}$, the set is non-empty; it is convex because convex combinations of non-decreasing functions with values in $[0,1]$ are again non-decreasing with values in $[0,1]$. For closedness, suppose $[f_n]\in\mathcal{C}$ and $[f_n]\to[f]$ in $L^2([a,b])$. Choose bounded non-decreasing representatives of $[f_n]$ and a subsequence converging almost everywhere to a representative of $[f]$. On the full-measure convergence set, the limit is non-decreasing; its monotone extension to $[a,b]$, obtained from one-sided suprema and endpoint limits, agrees with that representative almost everywhere and remains in $[0,1]$. Hence $[f]\in\mathcal{C}$. Because $\mathcal{C}$ is non-empty, closed, and convex in the Hilbert space $L^2([a,b])$, its metric projection $P_{\mathcal{C}}:L^2([a,b])\to\mathcal{C}$ exists, is unique at the equivalence-class level, and is $1$-Lipschitz.

    For (ii), with $G_s$ as above and $u\in L^2([a,b])$, let $h_u(y)=\int_a^b u(x)\mathbbm{1}\{y\leq x\}\,\mathrm{d}x$. Since $\langle\mathbb{E}[\chi_t\mid\mathcal{F}_s],u\rangle=\mathbb{E}[\langle\chi_t,u\rangle\mid\mathcal{F}_s]$ almost surely, Fubini's theorem for the kernel $\kappa_s$ gives $\langle\mathbb{E}[\chi_t\mid\mathcal{F}_s],u\rangle=\mathbb{E}[h_u(X_t)\mid\mathcal{F}_s]=\int_a^b u(x)G_s(\cdot,x)\,\mathrm{d}x$ almost surely. Applying this to a countable dense subset of $L^2([a,b])$ and discarding countably many null sets gives $\mathbb{E}[\chi_t\mid\mathcal{F}_s]=[G_s(\cdot,\cdot)|_{[a,b]}]$ almost surely. Since each $G_s(\omega,\cdot)$ is a distribution function, $\mathbb{E}[\chi_t\mid\mathcal{F}_s]\in\mathcal{C}$ almost surely.

    For (iii), for any $[f]\in\mathcal{C}$, the selected extension $\mathsf{S}([f])$ is non-decreasing and right-continuous, has limits $0$ and $1$ at $-\infty$ and $+\infty$, and may assign masses at $a$ and $b$; it therefore lies in $\mathfrak{D}_{[a,b]}$. By construction, $\mathsf{S}$ is the inverse of the restriction map $F\mapsto[F|_{[a,b]}]$ from $\mathfrak{D}_{[a,b]}$ to $\mathcal{C}$, so the $L^2([a,b])$ encoding of distribution functions supported on $[a,b]$ is injective. Since any two distribution functions $F,G\in\mathfrak{D}_{[a,b]}$ agree outside $[a,b)$, their Cram\'er distance $(\int_{\mathbb{R}}(F-G)^2\,\mathrm{d}x)^{1/2}$ equals $\lVert[F|_{[a,b]}]-[G|_{[a,b]}]\rVert_{L^2([a,b])}$, which proves that $\mathsf{S}$ is an isometry.
